sentences.text: 2  ORDER

Petitioner challenges the order dated 01-09-2018, taking cognizance of only the offence under section 323 of the Indian Penal Code 1860 (for short IPC) and also seeks a direction for taking cognizance of the offences under sections 498A and 294(b) IPC.
2.
Petitioner was the defacto complainant in Crime No.1593 of 2017 of Palarivattam Police Station.
The FIR was registered alleging offences under Sections 498A, 294(b) and 323 read with Section 34 of IPC.
In the complaint filed by the petitioner, there were specific allegations that the first accused-the husband of the defacto complainant had harassed her with demands for property.
Allegations were levelled against five other accused as well.
There were also specific allegations regarding injuries caused to her on account of the assault by the first accused.
During the investigation also, petitioner reiterated the said allegations, especially with regard to the first accused.

However, when the final report was filed, the police deleted the offences under sections 498A and 34 of the IPC and filed a report only against the first accused, that too, for the offences under Sections 294(b) and 323 IPC.

Pursuant to the final report, without giving any information to the informant regarding the deletion of the CRL.MC NO. 8126 OF 2019 offence under Section 498A IPC and also the removal of five persons from the array of accused, the learned Magistrate took cognizance only for the offence under Section 323 IPC by the impugned order dated 01.09.2018.
Petitioner challenges the said order.

3. I have heard Sri. P.K Rakesh Kumar on behalf of Sri. K.S. Madhusoodanan, the learned counsel for the petitioner, Sri.Noushad K.A., the learned Public Prosecutor, and Sri. T. D Robin, the learned counsel for respondents 3 to 8.
4.

In the complaint filed by the petitioner, there were specific allegations of cruelty meted out to her,
especially by her husband for her failure to meet demands for property.
The said statement has been reiterated as is noticed from the section 161 Cr.P.C statement given by her.
However, when the final report was filed, curiously, the offence under Section 498A IPC was deleted from the list of offences.

In this context, this Court bears in mind that the husband of the petitioner is a police officer and the investigating officer has given no plausible reason to omit section 498A IPC.
5.

However, when the final report was considered by the learned Magistrate, cognizance was taken only for the offence under section 323 IPC and refused to take cognizance for the offence under section 294(b) IPC which was included in the final report.

The petitioner as the informant was not given any notice while filing the final report or when the cognizance was taken only for one of the two offences reported by the CRL.MC NO. 8126 OF 2019 police.

6. In the decision in Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police and Another [AIR 1985 SC 1285],
the Supreme Court has observed that when the Magistrate decides not to take cognizance of the offence or drop the proceeding or takes the view that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against some of the persons mentioned in the First Information Report, the Magistrate must give notice to the informant and provide him an opportunity to be heard at the time of consideration of the report.

entities.text: Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police and Another [AIR 1985 SC 1285]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
After narrating the procedure to be followed while considering the final report, it was Nimisha Simon vs State Of Kerala on 10 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115280229/
3 observed that:-
"if the Magistrate decides that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding further and drops the proceeding or takes the view that though there is sufficient ground for proceeding against some, there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against others mentioned in the first information.

entities.text: Nimisha Simon vs State Of Kerala
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: report, the informant would certainly be prejudiced because the first information.
report lodged by him would have failed its purpose, wholly or in part.

Moreover, when the interest of the informant in prompt and effective action being taken on the first information report lodged by him is clearly recognised by the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of Section 154, sub- section (2) of Section 157 and sub-section (2) (ii) of Section 173, it must be presumed that the informant would equally be interested in seeing that the Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence and issues process because that would be culmination of the first information report lodged by him.
There can.

therefore, be no doubt that when, on a consideration of the report made by the officer-in- charge of a police station under sub-section (2)(i) of Section 173, the Magistrate is not inclined to take cognizance of the offence and issue process, the informant must be given an opportunity of being CRL.MC NO. 8126 OF 2019 heard so that he can make his submissions to persuade the Magistrate to take cognizance of the offence and issue process.

We are accordingly of the view that in a case where the Magistrate to whom a report is forwarded under sub-section (2)(i) of Section 173 decides not to take cognizance of the offence and to drop the proceeding or takes the view that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against some of the persons mentioned in the first information report, the Magistrate must give notice to the informant and provide him an opportunity to be heard at the time of consideration of the report."

7. In the instant case, as mentioned earlier, though the complaint alleged offences under sections 498A, 294(b) and 323 IPC, the final report was filed alleging offences under Sections 294(b) and 323 IPC, while the learned Magistrate proceeded to take cognizance only for the offence under Section 323 IPC.
Therefore, the petitioner ought to have been given notice before the learned Magistrate took cognizance of only one of the offences.

I am fortified in the above view by the decision of this Court in Usha John v. State of Kerala and Others [MANU/KE/0351/2005].
8.

entities.text: Usha John v. State of Kerala and Others [MANU/KE/0351/2005]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In this context, it needs to be mentioned that the learned Magistrate has acted mechanically in taking cognizance of the offence without applying his mind even to the final report.

When the complainant had specifically alleged that the accused had committed cruelty on her by demanding money and the offence of Section 498A IPC could have been made out, police deleted the said offence while filing the final report.
The learned Magistrate before proceeding to take cognizance of the matter CRL.MC NO. 8126 OF 2019 could have certainly considered whether the matter required a further investigation.
However, bearing in mind the jurisdiction exercised by this Court and the nature of relief that is proposed to be issued, I say no more.
Considering the circumstances, I am of the view that the order taking cognizance ought to be set aside and the learned Magistrate should consider the final report afresh.
